clue.text: I'm right out of sweeteners for drinks

indicators.note: 'out of' says the letter standing for right has gone missing from the word that follows

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
R is the standard abbreviation for right
bribes sweeten an official, so they are slang sweeteners

explanation.surface: Someone declares they have run out of sugar substitutes for their drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweeteners' looks like sugar for the drinks, but it is slang for illicit payments.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbibe is to drink, so the third-person verb form matches 'drinks' as a verb.

clue.text: Cycling coach on unknown — there might be some work to do here

definitions.text: there might be some work to do here

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round from the front to the back, so the word for coach is rotated

blocks.note: to coach someone is to train them
Y is one of the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: A cycling coach is riding with an unknown amount of work still waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: Move TR from the front of TRAIN to the back to get INTRA, then add Y.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-tray on a desk holds incoming papers still awaiting attention, so work may be waiting there.

clue.text: Perhaps Jo Whiley's last drink

indicators.note: 'last' keeps only the final letter of the surname it follows

blocks.note: Jo Brand is a British comedian, so a Jo might be a Brand
final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: Radio presenter Jo Whiley orders one final drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Jo Whiley is a BBC radio DJ, which pulls you towards one person; the clue splits her first name off to evoke the comedian Jo Brand instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine, a common alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Local's stuff regularly stolen by tyrant with evident pride

indicators.note: 'regularly' keeps letters at an even spacing, here every second one
what is stolen is taken inside by the thief, so one piece ends up within the other

blocks.note: a bully tyrannises others
second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A tyrant proudly makes off with a pub regular's belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is British slang for one's neighbourhood pub, and also a regular there; the possessive is part of the letter string.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting boastfully means showing off, displaying pride openly to others.

clue.text: Pervert is looking up skirts on catwalk shows essentially

indicators.note: in a down clue, looking up means the word reads from bottom to top
skirts are the edges of something, so only the outside letters are kept
the essence is the core, so only the central letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
first and last letters
middle letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A voyeur peers up models' skirts during fashion shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirts' looks like the object of the peeping, but it is the selector working on 'catwalk'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sicko is slang for a sick-minded person, and a pervert fits that description.

clue.text: Remains in church with tea for the audience — and cake

indicators.note: 'in' places one word inside the abbreviation for church
an audience hears rather than reads, so take the word by its sound

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
a rump is what remains of something larger
the letter T is said the same as the drink

explanation.surface: Leftovers served in church alongside tea and a cake for the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the tea is heard; the church abbreviation and the remains are taken as they are written.
explanation.definitionFit: A crumpet is a soft griddle cake eaten toasted with butter, a British teatime staple.

clue.text: 1 Down etc could be foregone conclusion

indicators.note: 'could be' says the letters might become something else once rearranged

blocks.note: the answer to 1 Down
taken as written

explanation.surface: An in-tray and suchlike could be a done deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'etc' looks like a vague continuation of the list, but its three letters join the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A foregone conclusion is an outcome already settled, which is a certainty.

clue.text: Exhausted masseuse drops trousers

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so these words keep the answer tucked inside them

blocks.note: the letters span the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A worn-out masseuse lets her trousers fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is a verb, meaning pockets, not the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Used, as in used up, means exhausted or consumed with nothing left.

clue.text: Impressionist returning under pressure to host series ultimately gets one in the can

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the painter's name runs the other way
a host takes a guest in, so one piece sits inside the other
'ultimately' means at the end, so only the final letter is used
in a down clue, being under something means following it

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a French Impressionist painter
last letter

explanation.surface: A returning stage impressionist hosts a series under pressure and ends up jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: An impressionist can be a mimic, but here it is the painter. RIONER takes S after its second letter, and P goes on top.
explanation.definitionFit: The can is slang for prison, so one inside it is an inmate.

clue.text: Seeing corporation before 9, say and pitching …

indicators.note: 'before' sets the first piece ahead of the second in the finished word

blocks.note: a corporation is old slang for a paunch, a belly
a tiara, the answer to 9 Across, is an example of flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: Spotting a pot-bellied figure ahead of number nine, then pitching about.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation in the sense of a large stomach is an old jokey British usage. 'Tumble to' is slang for realise, so tumbling means seeing; it also means falling headlong.
explanation.definitionFit: To tumble to something is to grasp it, and pitching forward is tumbling over.

clue.text: Crown and Anchor content to leave a pint every now and then on the counter

indicators.note: the contents leaving means the inside letters go, keeping only the shell
occasionally means only every other letter is kept
counter means contrary, so the assembled letters are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written before its insides are emptied
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Drinkers at the Crown and Anchor pub happily leave a pint on the bar now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Crown and Anchor reads as a pub name, but 'Crown' is the definition and 'and' a link. Emptying ANCHOR leaves AR; add AIT and reverse the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled coronet, a kind of small crown worn by women.

clue.text: Medicare reformed with President at the fore — go for it!

indicators.note: something reformed is formed anew, so its letters are rearranged
the fore is the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter

explanation.surface: A president leading a reform of the US Medicare health scheme is urged to seize the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Medicare is the US government health insurance scheme for older people.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpe diem is Latin for seize the day, an exhortation to act now.

clue.text: Villain discovered island in middle of Portland is spare

indicators.note: dis-covered means having its cover stripped, so the outer letters go
'in' sets the island inside the other piece
'middle of' keeps only the central letters of the place name

blocks.note: a baddie is the villain of a story
the two central letters of an eight-letter word
Iona is an island of the Inner Hebrides, Scotland

explanation.surface: A villain finds an island off Portland and calls it surplus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' looks like 'found', but it means stripped of its covering: BADDIE loses B and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare and additional both describe something extra beyond what is needed.

clue.text: Turkey say Foreign Office is oversharing with member of parliament

indicators.note: oversharing here means the two pieces overlap and share a letter, so one copy of it is dropped

blocks.note: FO is the abbreviation for the UK Foreign Office
a group of owls is called a parliament

explanation.surface: Turkey's foreign ministry is caught leaking too much to an MP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member of parliament' wants to be an MP, but it is a bird: owls gather in a parliament. FO and OWL share their O.
explanation.definitionFit: A turkey is an example of fowl, the domestic birds kept for meat and eggs.

clue.text: … crazy ideas about going on vacation — managed to get upgrade

indicators.note: crazy means disordered, so the letters are jumbled
a word on vacation is vacated, emptied, leaving only its ends
'about' means around, so the jumbled letters surround the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled
first and last letters
to run something is to manage it

explanation.surface: Mad notions about heading off on holiday led to an upgrade.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 8 Down for the surface only; this clue stands alone. Going on vacation means the word is emptied of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrandise is to raise something in rank or importance, to elevate or enhance it.

clue.text: Some links framing politician

blocks.note: framing words is putting them a certain way
a member of the Green Party

explanation.surface: A conspiracy-theory picture: several connections are setting up a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Links is a golf course, especially one by the sea; 'framing' looks like setting someone up but means phrasing.
explanation.definitionFit: A putting green is part of a golf course, so it is some of the links.

clue.text: Can Joe Root for example find help for Cook?

blocks.note: a tin is a can
Joe Root has batted in the top order for England; an opener starts the innings

explanation.surface: A question about whether England cricketer Joe Root can help his teammate Alastair Cook.
explanation.walkthrough: Alastair Cook was England's opening batsman, so the capital C points to cricket; in the definition it is just a kitchen cook.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin-opener is a kitchen gadget, a utensil that assists anyone preparing food.

clue.text: Group clever to control rising chaos

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, from bottom to top
to control something is to hold it, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: able means capable, clever
a mess is chaos

explanation.surface: A smart group sets out to rein in growing disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: Group must be read as a verb, to bring together.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather things or people together, forming a group.

clue.text: Swedes maybe in Costa Rica wearing shirt under jumper

indicators.note: something wearing a garment is inside it, so these letters go within
in a down clue, being under means coming after

blocks.note: a roo, kangaroo, is a jumper
a shirt is a top
CR is the international code for Costa Rica

explanation.surface: Swedish tourists in Costa Rica wear a shirt beneath a sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: Swedes are Swedish people on the surface, but a swede is a turnip-like vegetable (rutabaga). A jumper is British for a sweater, the false path here.
explanation.definitionFit: A swede is a vegetable grown for its edible root, an example of a root crop.

clue.text: Detectives seen in country garden

blocks.note: a country of the United Kingdom
yard is the American word for a garden

explanation.surface: Plain-clothes police are spotted in a country garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country garden' reads as a rural garden, but splits as two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police, standing for its detective branch.

clue.text: Rogue agents detaining six-footer

indicators.note: detaining someone holds them inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency
a cad is a rogue, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: Rogue spies hold a very tall man captive.
explanation.walkthrough: A six-footer sounds like a tall person, but it is any insect, which has six legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A cicada is a chirping insect, and insects have six legs.

clue.text: Shiny silver transformed meal

indicators.note: transformed means changed in form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Gleaming silverware has transformed an ordinary meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Agleam means gleaming or glowing, so shining brightly.

clue.text: Worries constituency making small move to the far right

indicators.text: making small move to the far right
indicators.note: the abbreviation for small travels from the front to the very end of the word

blocks.note: a parliamentary constituency is a seat

explanation.surface: Concern that a constituency is swinging to the far right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'far right' sounds political, but it means the end of the word; S stands for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats, as in what's eating you, means troubles or bothers someone.

clue.text: Honest courier setting down parcel finally dropped off on time

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the end letter of the word it follows
dropped off means discarded, so that letter is removed
in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: UPS is a parcel delivery company
T is the abbreviation for time
landing a plane is setting it down
last letter

explanation.surface: An honest courier puts the parcel down and drops it off on time.
explanation.walkthrough: LANDING loses its L, then the remainder follows T.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstanding person is honest and respectable, a pillar of the community.

clue.text: Pop music to dance to?

blocks.note: first meaning: a British brand of fizzy orange soft drink, pop being fizzy drink
second meaning: a Latin American ballroom dance and its music

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop music' looks like one phrase; it splits after 'Pop'. Tango is a fizzy drink sold in Britain, and pop is everyday British for fizzy drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an Argentine dance, with its music, and a branded soda.

clue.text: Reasonable ticket price announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so take the word by its sound

blocks.note: the fare is what a travel ticket costs

explanation.surface: A sensible ticket price has been declared.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair means just and reasonable, as in a fair deal.

clue.text: Expect profit working next to pub

indicators.note: 'next to' places the pub beside the other pieces, here at the front

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
gain is profit
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Someone anticipates profits from a job beside a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To bargain on something is to count on it, to anticipate it happening.

clue.text: Silly grandparent appearing in Viz

indicators.note: appearing in something means being inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: viz and i.e. both mean namely
nan is a grandmother

explanation.surface: A daft granny turns up in the comic Viz.
explanation.walkthrough: Viz is a crude British comic magazine, but here it is the Latin abbreviation meaning namely.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means senseless or foolish, a synonym for silly.

clue.text: Theatre in capital brought back Mikado

indicators.note: 'in' puts the theatre inside the city
brought back means returned, so the whole reads the other way

blocks.note: Rome is the capital of Italy
rep is repertory theatre

explanation.surface: A theatre in the capital has revived The Mikado.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado is the Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera, but the title also means the emperor of Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikado was the old title of the Japanese emperor.

clue.text: One way to make deliveries — pack too much?

blocks.note: first meaning: a bowling or throwing style with the arm brought over the shoulder
second meaning: to arm, or pack with weapons, excessively

explanation.walkthrough: Deliveries are cricket balls bowled, not parcels; 'pack' means to carry weapons, as in packing a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a cricket bowling action and also, split, a verb for giving too many weapons.
